newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei falls as turnover hits year's low.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei falls as turnover hits year's low.

text.p: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 stock average closed sharply lower on Monday, battered by bouts of futures-linked selling, with the losses magnified by slack turnover which hit a low for the year, brokers said.
"The end of the month is approaching and important economic indicators are due out this week, keeping participants away," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities.
The benchmark 225-Nikkei average tumbled 345.06 points, or 1.63 percent, to settle at 20,883.74.
Turnover totalled a weak 211.66 million shares at the end of the session. The previous low was set on August 16 when trade totalled 214 million shares.
The Nikkei average had been on a four-day winning streak last week, before tripping on Friday.
"The Nikkei average and its September futures ended in backwardation on Friday, inviting the unwinding of arbitrage-linked positions this morning," one broker said.
September futures settled 300 points down at 20,910.
Arbitrageurs simultaneously trade stocks and their underlying futures, and profit from momentary discrepancies between the prices of the two instruments.

Brokers said that on top of Japanese indicators due this week, interest rate-hike fears were haunting the market once again after the U.S. long bond yield leaped to 6.93 percent on Friday, its highest level since July 31.

"Some participants are beginning to think that perhaps a rate hike in the U.S. is not so far away after all and that is giving them a case of cold feet," Ryoichi Ohta, general manager at Tokyo Securities said.
Brokers said the market basically agreed that the Bank of Japan's survey on corporate sentiment, due out on Wednesday, would not reveal anything startling.
"With ripples of tension coming from Wall Street, the market wants reassurance before heading off in a certain direction," one broker said.
However, July industrial production figures scheduled for Friday are widely expected to be better than the lower-than-expected June figures, adding to the anxiety.
"We want to know just how much better the data is before doing anything," he said.
